It's the perfect mechanism for pistols, and I really wish it was more popular. The Browning tilting-barrel action is all right, but it has more than its share of limitations, and I think the main reason manufacturers are sticking with it is laziness and inertia. With a gas-delayed blowback, you get:

  • A fixed barrel. The most obvious benefit is increased potential accuracy--less less moving parts means more consistency, which means better accuracy. The other, less immediately visible benefit is the ability to use dual-feed magazines, which tilting-barrel actions can't easily do. A dual-feed magazine, like what most rifles use, will provide fewer failures to feed than the double-stack/single-feed magazines found in most pistols today. They're also a lot easier to load.

  • Less complexity. There are fewer moving parts required to make the system, making field maintenance relatively easy. And if you do what Steyr did with the GB, and make the barrel pull double duty as the gas piston, the mechanism is even simpler. This both makes maintenance easier, and reduces the number of failure points, which increases reliability. This also makes manufacturing easier, assuming you have good machinists with good quality control, and don't churn out shit copy guns that destroy reputations like Rogak did.

  • Low bore-axis. Without the need to leave space under the barrel for it to tilt down, you can get the barrel much lower in the frame, and more in line with the shooter's grip, which reduces muzzle flip. If you put the recoil spring above the barrel, which is what Laugo Arms did with their new Alien pistol, you can get it even lower.

  • Low recoil. Because the gas piston in gas-delayed blowback systems is applying force in the direction opposite the slide's movement, it reduces the force of recoil felt by the shooter.

  • Ammo flexibility. Unlike other delayed blowback systems, gas-delayed is not tuned to work with a very specific load, but will self-regulate to work with all variety of loads. If it's hotter ammo, pressure in the piston will be higher, and the delaying force on the slide will be higher--just what you need for a hotter load. Conversely, weaker loads that produce lower pressure will see lower pressure on the piston, making it easier for the slide to go back. This is unlike lever or roller-delayed blowback, which usually need to be tuned to a specific type of ammunition.

There are only two real disadvantages of gas-delay, and they can be mitigated: heat and fouling. The gasses coming out of the barrel port are real hot, and understandably they can heat up the gun, especially if you put the port close to the grip like HK did with the P7. But you can just do what was done with the Steyr GB, and move the delay system forward a bit, so the port isn't spraying hot gas directly over the grip. The fouling can be annoying to clean, but as long as the gun itself is robust and well-designed, it doesn't get in the way of reliability. See: AR-15, HK's roller-delayed actions.
